questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that each turn one list into a new list with a single comprehension.

How this works in Python

Java gives you two ways to build a list out of another list. The first is the loop you reach for without thinking.

List<Integer> doubled = new ArrayList<>();
for (int value : values) {
    doubled.add(value * 2);
}

The second is the stream pipeline.

List<Integer> doubled = values.stream()
        .filter(value -> value > 0)
        .map(value -> value * 2)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

Python replaces both with one piece of syntax, the list comprehension.

doubled = [value * 2 for value in values]

That is the whole thing. There is no builder to declare, no stream to open, no collector to close, and no boxing between int and Integer. This is the most Python-shaped construct in the language, and a reader who knows Python expects to see it wherever one list becomes another.

The three parts

Every comprehension has an output expression and a for clause. The filter on the end is optional.

[ value * 2   for value in values   if value > 0 ]
  ---------   -------------------   ------------
  output      for clause            filter
  expression                        optional
  runs once   binds each item       decides which
  per item    to a name             items survive

The for value in values part is the same for header you already write as a statement, so it takes each item of values in turn and binds it to value. The expression in front of the for then runs once for each item, and whatever it produces becomes one item of the new list. The input list is never touched, and what you get back is a new list.

Turning your loop into one

Any loop that starts with an empty list and appends one item per pass converts mechanically. Three lines go in, one comes out.

doubled = []                       # throw this line away
for value in values:               # this becomes the for clause
    doubled.append(value * 2)      # what you append becomes the output expression

doubled = [value * 2 for value in values]

Do that transformation on paper the first few times. The pieces never move about, they only change places. The thing being appended goes to the front, and the loop header follows it.

The filter

Put an if on the end and items start getting dropped.

positives = [value for value in values if value > 0]

An item that fails the test never reaches the expression at the front, so that one word does the entire job of .filter(...). It sits last, where Java puts filter first. When the stream order helps you, read the Python right to left. Take the values, keep the ones above zero, double whatever is left.

Look at what the output expression is doing in that line. It is the loop variable on its own, because you want the item unchanged. [value for value in values ...] reads as though somebody typed the same word twice by mistake. It is correct. The first value is what gets built, and the second is what gets bound.

An expression, not a statement

A Java for loop is a statement and produces nothing, so a method that builds a list needs a local variable to catch the result. A comprehension is an expression, which means it produces a value. It fits straight after a return with no variable in between.

def doubled(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [value * 2 for value in values]

The first test prints the input list after doubled has run, so you can see for yourself that the original survived.

Your task
  • doubled(values) returns a new list holding every value multiplied by two. The answer box already holds the loop version. Delete its three lines and write the comprehension.
  • positives(values) returns only the values above zero, unchanged. Output expression and filter, no arithmetic.
  • shouted(words) returns every word in upper case. word.upper() hands you an upper case copy, from the strings topic.
  • long_shouts(words) returns the words of five characters or more, in upper case. All three parts at once.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not write the word append anywhere. A hidden test looks for it.
  • Do not call map() or filter(). The comprehension is what replaced them.
  • One def line and one return line per function, and nothing else. A hidden test counts them.
  • Annotate every signature, parameters and return alike. Write list[int], never List[int], because the capitalised spelling has been dead since Python 3.9.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: import inspect for fn in (doubled, positives, shouted, long_shouts): src = inspect.getsource(fn) body = [ln for ln in src.splitlines() if ln.strip() and not ln.strip().startswith("#")] assert len(body) == 2, "rule broken: one def line and one return line, nothing else" assert "append(" not in src, "rule broken: the word append must not appear" assert "map(" not in src, "rule broken: do not call map()" assert "filter(" not in src, "rule broken: do not call filter()" print(positives([-2, -1])) print(shouted([])) print(long_shouts(["short", "tiny"])) print(doubled([0]))

name.text: WAT 13.2: One Line to Rule Them All!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that each use one list comprehension over a list of readings.

How this works in Python

Java gives you two ways to build a list out of another list. The loop.

List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
for (int r : readings) {
    result.add(r * 10);
}

And the stream.

List<Integer> result = readings.stream()
        .map(r -> r * 10)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

Python replaces both with one piece of syntax. It is called a list comprehension. It is an expression rather than a statement, so it produces a value and fits on the right of an = or straight after a return.

result = [r * 10 for r in readings]

Read it left to right. The square brackets build a list. The for r in readings part takes each item of readings in turn and binds it to r, exactly as the for statement from the loops topic does. The expression sitting in front of the for builds one item per pass. You get a new list back and readings is left alone. There is no stream to open, no collector to close, and no boxing between int and Integer.

Put an if at the end and the comprehension filters.

result = [r * 10 for r in readings if r >= 0]

The trailing if decides which items survive. An item that fails the test never reaches the expression at the front. That one word does the whole job of .filter(...), and it comes last where Java's filter comes first.

A filter throws items away. Sometimes you want to keep every item and change some of them. Java writes that choice with the ternary operator.

int safe = r < 0 ? 0 : r;

Python writes the same choice with words, in a different order.

safe = 0 if r < 0 else r

Java puts the condition first. Python puts the value you want first, then the condition, then the alternative. Say it out loud as "zero if the reading is negative, otherwise the reading" and the order stops surprising you. This form is called a conditional expression. You met it in the truth and None topic. It produces a value, so it goes in front of the for.

result = [0 if r < 0 else r for r in readings]

Two if words, two different jobs. An if before the for chooses a value and keeps every item. An if after the for drops items. Write a bare filter at the front and Python raises SyntaxError.

One more difference, and it catches people in real code. A plain Python for statement leaves its variable behind after the loop ends. In the lines below, pass is Python's do-nothing statement. It is there because every block needs a body.

for r in readings:
    pass
print(r)              # prints the last reading

Java never does that. A variable declared in a for header dies with the loop. A Python comprehension behaves the way you expect from Java. Its variable lives inside the brackets and goes when they close. Ask for it afterwards and Python raises NameError. The last function below makes you prove it.

Your task

Readings arrive as a list of whole numbers.

  • scaled(readings) returns a new list holding every reading multiplied by 10. The answer box already holds a working loop. Delete all four of its lines and write one comprehension.
  • in_range(readings) returns only the readings from 0 to 100 inclusive. Anything outside that band is dropped.
  • floored(readings) keeps every reading, but a reading below 0 becomes 0. Nothing is dropped, so the returned list is always as long as the input.
  • leak_check(readings) builds [n * n for n in readings] into a variable called squares, then proves that n is gone. Read n inside a try block. Catch the failure with except NameError as problem. Return f"{squares} and n is gone: {problem}". Name the comprehension variable n or the printed text will not match.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write scaled, in_range and floored as one return line each. A hidden test counts the lines.
  • Do not write the word append anywhere.
  • Do not call map() or filter(). The comprehension is what replaced them.
  • Do not write an if statement. The trailing filter and the a if cond else b form are the only if words allowed.
  • Annotate every signature you write, parameters and return alike. Write list[int], never List[int], because the capitalised spelling has been dead since Python 3.9.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

expected.text: [9, 16] and n is gone: name 'n' is not defined [] [] []

testcode.text: import inspect for fn in (scaled, in_range, floored): src = inspect.getsource(fn) body = [ln for ln in src.splitlines() if ln.strip() and not ln.strip().startswith("#")] assert len(body) == 2, "rule broken: one def line and one return line, nothing else" assert "append(" not in src, "rule broken: the word append must not appear" assert "map(" not in src, "rule broken: do not call map()" assert "filter(" not in src, "rule broken: do not call filter()" print(scaled([-1, 7])) print(in_range([-1, 0, 100, 101])) print(floored([-9, -1, 0, 1])) print(leak_check([2]))

expected.text: [-10, 70] [0, 100] [0, 0, 0, 1] [4] and n is gone: name 'n' is not defined

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that each build a dict or a set with one comprehension.

How this works in Python

In Java you build a map with a loop and put.

Map<String, String> flipped = new HashMap<>();
for (Map.Entry<String, String> entry : codes.entrySet()) {
    flipped.put(entry.getValue(), entry.getKey());
}

Python has a dict comprehension. It works the same way as the list comprehension in the earlier tiers of this topic, with two changes. The outer brackets are braces, and the item you build is a key: value pair.

flipped = {name: code for code, name in codes.items()}

codes.items() hands you one (key, value) tuple per entry, as you saw in the dictionaries and sets topic. The two names code, name in the header take that tuple apart and bind each half to a name. Taking a sequence apart into names is unpacking, from the tuples topic. No entrySet, no getKey, no getValue.

Drop the colon and the braces build a set instead. A set holds distinct values in no particular order, and you met it alongside dictionaries.

units = {record["unit"] for record in records}

One warning about braces. Empty braces {} mean an empty dict, never an empty set. A set comprehension with nothing to collect still gives you a set, so the trap catches you only when you type the empty literal yourself.

Now the part that costs people data. Java's Collectors.toMap refuses to guess.

codes.entrySet().stream()
     .collect(Collectors.toMap(Map.Entry::getValue, Map.Entry::getKey));
// IllegalStateException: Duplicate key sensor

Java makes you supply a merge function before it will accept a collision. Python does not ask. When two entries produce the same key, the later one overwrites the earlier one and nothing is raised. You saw the same last-wins rule when a repeated key overwrote its own entry. An inversion is where it hurts most. A mapping of three codes to two names inverts into two entries, and the third code is gone.

The honest repair is to make the value a list. Then every key keeps everything that mapped to it.

{name: [code for code, other in mapping.items() if other == name]
 for name in mapping.values()}

Look at the outer for. It walks mapping.values(), which repeats a value once per code. That repeat is harmless. It rebuilds the same key with the same list, so the second write stores what the first write stored. You get one entry per distinct value, in the order the values first appeared. Yes, this is a comprehension inside a comprehension. The inner one runs once for every pass of the outer one.

The tests print the size of a mapping before and after invert. The loss shows up on screen as a number rather than as a bug you find in production.

Your task
  • index_of(names) takes a list of names and returns {name: position}, where the first name maps to 0. You need the position, and your only tool for that so far is range(len(names)) from the loops topic. So walk the positions and index the list inside the braces. Remember how clumsy this feels. The next exercise deletes it forever.
  • distinct_units(records) takes a list of dicts, each with an "id" key and a "unit" key, and returns the set of distinct units.
  • by_id(records) returns a dict mapping each record's "id" to the whole record.
  • invert(mapping) takes a {code: name} dict and returns {name: code}. Write the lossy version. Do not defend it.
  • group_by_value(mapping) takes the same kind of dict and returns {name: [codes]}, keeping every code. The codes stay in the order they appear in the input.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Write every answer as one expression whose outer brackets are braces.
  • Do not call dict(), set() or zip().
  • Do not create an empty dict and fill it in a loop. If a line other than a def line ends with a colon, start again.
  • Do not make invert safe. Let it lose the duplicate, then keep everything in group_by_value.
  • Annotate every signature. A function that hands back dict[str, list[str]] should say so on its first line, not leave you to read the comprehension and guess.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: codes = {"E01": "sensor", "E02": "valve"} print(invert(codes)) faults = {"E01": "sensor", "E02": "valve", "E03": "sensor"} flipped = invert(faults) print(f"{len(faults)} codes in, {len(flipped)} names out") print(flipped) print(group_by_value(faults))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (index_of, distinct_units, by_id, invert, group_by_value)) assert "dict(" not in whole, "rule broken: no dict()" assert "set(" not in whole, "rule broken: no set()" assert "zip(" not in whole, "rule broken: no zip()" assert "append(" not in whole, "rule broken: no append" for line in whole.splitlines(): text = line.strip() assert not text.endswith(":") or text.startswith("def "), "rule broken: no loop body, no colon ending a line" print(index_of([])) print(sorted(distinct_units([]))) print(group_by_value({})) print(group_by_value({"a": 1, "b": 1, "c": 2})) print(invert({"a": 1, "b": 1}))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that walk lists with enumerate and zip instead of an index.

How this works in Python

Java keeps the index loop alive for one reason. You need the position.

for (int i = 0; i < lines.size(); i++) {
    System.out.println((i + 1) + ": " + lines.get(i));
}

Python hands you the position and the item together, through enumerate.

for position, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
    print(f"{position}: {line}")

enumerate(lines) produces a (position, item) tuple for every item. start=1 says the first position is 1 instead of 0. The two names in the header unpack the tuple. Nothing is indexed and no counter is added by hand, so a position can never drift out of step with the item beside it.

Java gives you no way to walk two collections side by side. You index both and you keep the bounds right yourself.

for (int i = 0; i < channels.size(); i++) {
    table.put(channels.get(i), readings.get(i));
}

Python has zip. It takes two or more iterables and produces one tuple per position. An iterable is anything you can put after in in a for statement, so a list, a tuple, a dict and a range all qualify.

table = {channel: reading for channel, reading in zip(channels, readings)}

Read the next sentence twice. zip stops at the shortest input and says nothing. Pass three channels and two readings and you get a table of two rows, no error, no warning. In a safety system that is a reading that disappeared between the sensor and the report.

Since Python 3.10 you can refuse that behaviour.

zip(channels, readings, strict=True)

With strict=True, a length mismatch raises ValueError the moment zip runs off the end of the shorter input. Loud beats quiet. Every zip in this exercise passes it.

zip also transposes. Put a star in front of a list of rows. Each row then arrives as a separate argument. That is the starred call from the tuples topic.

rows = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
zip(*rows, strict=True)        # same as zip([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], strict=True)

The first item of every row groups together, then the second item of every row, and so on. That is a transpose. Each group comes back as a tuple, so wrap it in list(...) when you want lists.

Last piece. A comprehension can carry more than one for clause, and the clauses read in the same order as nested loops.

flat = [value for row in rows for value in row]

The first for takes a row. The second walks that row. The expression at the front sees the innermost variable. Beginners often write nested brackets here and get a list of lists back. The brackets stay on the outside and only the for clauses repeat.

One test calls pair with a readings list one item short. It prints the name of the exception instead of the two rows a silent zip would have produced.

Your task
  • numbered(lines) takes a list of alert lines and returns a list of strings of the form "1: pressure high", numbered from 1.
  • pair(channels, readings) returns a dict mapping each channel to its reading. Pass strict=True.
  • flatten(rows) takes a list of rows and returns one flat list of every value, row by row.
  • transpose(rows) returns a list of lists where the first inner list holds the first value of every row, the second holds the second, and so on.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • The characters range(len( must never appear.
  • Do not increment a counter of your own. enumerate owns the position now.
  • Pass strict=True to every zip call. Silent truncation is a defect, not a convenience.
  • Do not index with square brackets. Unpack both values in the loop header instead.
  • Flatten with one comprehension holding two for clauses. Do not nest brackets and do not call sum().
  • Annotate every signature, and both of pair's parameters. Nobody should have to run the tests to find out that transpose hands back list[list[int]].
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: lines = ["pressure high", "valve stuck", "temp drift"] for line in numbered(lines): print(line) print(pair(["ch1", "ch2", "ch3"], [12, 7, 30]))

expected.text: 1: pressure high 2: valve stuck 3: temp drift {'ch1': 12, 'ch2': 7, 'ch3': 30}

testcode.text: try: print(pair(["ch1", "ch2", "ch3"], [12, 7])) except ValueError as problem: print("strict caught it:", type(problem).__name__) matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] print(flatten(matrix)) print(transpose(matrix))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (numbered, pair, flatten, transpose)) assert "range(len(" not in whole, "rule broken: range(len( is banned" assert "+= 1" not in whole, "rule broken: do not increment a counter of your own" assert "sum(" not in whole, "rule broken: sum(rows, []) is not flattening" assert whole.count("zip(") == whole.count("strict=True"), "rule broken: every zip passes strict=True" assert inspect.getsource(flatten).count(" for ") == 2, "rule broken: one comprehension, two for clauses" print(numbered([])) print(numbered(["only"])) print(flatten([[9]])) print(flatten([])) print(transpose([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])) print(pair([], []))
